title: Language Variation and Dialects
description: Why everyone speaks differently — and what that reveals

concepts.title: What Is a Dialect?
concepts.contentHtml:
A dialect is a variety of a language that differs from others in vocabulary, grammar, and/or pronunciation — but is mutually intelligible with them (to varying degrees). All dialects are linguistically equal; none is 'better' or more 'correct' than others.

The famous quip (attributed variously): 'A language is a dialect with an army and a navy.' Whether two varieties count as dialects or separate languages is often political, not purely linguistic. Mandarin and Cantonese are called 'dialects' of Chinese politically — but they are mutually unintelligible. Norwegian and Swedish are called 'languages' but are mutually intelligible.

Every speaker has an idiolect — their individual unique variety. Social groups share a sociolect (social dialect), and regions share regional dialects.

concepts.title: Labov's Department Store Study
concepts.contentHtml:
William Labov is the founder of variationist sociolinguistics. His 1966 New York City study examined how speakers vary the use of post-vocalic /r/ (in words like 'fourth floor') across social classes and contexts.

He visited three department stores of different prestige (Saks Fifth Avenue, Macy's, S. Klein) and asked for items on the fourth floor to elicit the phrase with post-vocalic /r/. Higher-prestige stores showed more /r/ pronunciation. Workers in each store used more /r/ when asked to repeat ('Excuse me?'), showing style-shifting: speakers adjust their speech to context.

Labov showed that variation is not random or degenerate — it is systematic and socially meaningful. The variation itself encodes information about identity, class, and context.

concepts.title: Regional Dialects and Dialect Continua
concepts.contentHtml:
Dialect features spread geographically and create dialect continua: adjacent areas differ slightly, but the ends of the continuum may be mutually unintelligible. The Dutch-German dialect continuum runs from the Netherlands into southern Germany — a traveler moving through would hear gradual change at each village, but Amsterdam Dutch and Bavarian German are not mutually intelligible.

Isoglosses are lines on a map separating areas with different linguistic features. When many isoglosses cluster together, they form a bundle of isoglosses marking a dialect boundary. The classic US 'cot-caught merger' divides regions where these words are pronounced the same vs differently.

Dialect surveys (e.g., the Dictionary of American Regional English) systematically map lexical variation: soda vs pop vs coke for carbonated drinks varies strongly by US region.

title: Language and Identity
description: How language marks who we are — and who we want to be

concepts.title: Social Variables — Class, Gender, Age
concepts.contentHtml:
Sociolinguistics has established that linguistic variation correlates systematically with social variables:

Social class: Labov's NYC work showed /r/ use tracked social class. Peter Trudgill's Norwich study found that working-class speakers use more non-standard forms, especially in casual speech. Middle-class speakers show hypercorrection in formal contexts (over-applying prestige norms).

Gender: research consistently finds women use more standard prestige forms in formal contexts. Explanations vary — some point to social pressure, others to women being more sensitive to social evaluation. Men use more non-standard forms, associated with covert prestige (toughness, solidarity).

Age: speakers often retain features of the dialect they acquired in adolescence, creating age-graded variation. Younger speakers lead sound changes.

concepts.title: Language as Identity Performance
concepts.contentHtml:
Language is not just a communication tool — it is a performance of identity. We signal who we are (class, region, group affiliation, aspirations) through how we speak.

Penelope Eckert's work in Michigan high schools showed that 'Jocks' and 'Burnouts' (social categories) systematically differed in their participation in the Northern Cities Vowel Shift — Burnouts, who identified with the urban working class, led the change; Jocks, oriented toward institutional norms, lagged behind.

Speakers actively use linguistic features to construct identity. This is not conscious in most cases — but choices about vocabulary, slang, accent, and register all signal group membership. Language is always partly a declaration: I am one of these people.

concepts.title: Prestige — Overt and Covert
concepts.contentHtml:
Prestige in sociolinguistics refers to the social value attached to a language variety. Overt prestige belongs to standard or 'educated' varieties — the forms taught in school, used in formal contexts, openly valued. Speakers orient toward these forms in formal situations.

Covert prestige is the hidden social value of non-standard forms within peer groups. Working-class or vernacular features signal authenticity, toughness, solidarity, and in-group belonging. Speakers who abandon these features may be seen as 'putting on airs' or betraying their community.

Both types of prestige are real and functional. A speaker navigating between formal and informal contexts is balancing two prestige systems simultaneously. Language attitude surveys (matched-guise tests) measure both: speakers evaluate recordings of the same person using different varieties and reveal their attitudes indirectly.

title: Code-Switching and Multilingualism
description: How bilinguals mix languages — and why it's skilled, not confused

concepts.title: What Is Code-Switching?
concepts.contentHtml:
Code-switching is the practice of moving between two or more languages or dialects within a conversation — sometimes within a single sentence. It is common among bilinguals and multilingual communities worldwide.

'Voy al store porque necesito some milk.' (Spanish-English switching: 'I'm going to the store because I need some milk.') — Spanglish, common in US Latino communities.

Code-switching is not sloppy, confused, or degenerate speech. Research (Poplack, Myers-Scotton) shows it follows grammatical constraints — speakers never switch in ways that violate the grammar of either language. It requires high competence in both codes. Code-switchers are displaying linguistic skill, not deficiency.

concepts.title: Motivations for Code-Switching
concepts.contentHtml:
Speakers switch codes for many reasons, often simultaneously:

  • Topic: discussing work in English, family matters in heritage language
  • Addressee: switching to include or exclude a participant
  • Solidarity and identity: switching signals group membership (using Mandarin slang in an English-dominant conversation marks Chinese identity)
  • Quotation: reporting what someone said in the language they used
  • Lexical gap: the other language has a more precise word

Carol Myers-Scotton's markedness model: speakers choose codes by their 'markedness' in the situation — the expected code is unmarked; departing from it is marked and communicates something. Switching is always a meaning-making choice.

concepts.title: Diglossia and Language Choice
concepts.contentHtml:
Charles Ferguson (1959) coined diglossia to describe situations where two varieties of the same language are used for different social functions, with strict norms:

  • High (H) variety: formal, prestigious, learned in school — Arabic Modern Standard (fuṣḥā), Swiss Standard German, Katharevousa Greek
  • Low (L) variety: everyday speech, acquired at home — Egyptian Arabic, Swiss German (Schweizerdeutsch), Demotic Greek

Extended diglossia (Joshua Fishman) applies to socially distinct languages in a bilingual community (e.g., Spanish/English in Puerto Rico). Diglossia is functional — both varieties serve real social roles. Attempts to replace L entirely with H often fail; people need a language for intimate, informal life.

title: AAVE, Pidgins, Creoles, and Contact Languages
description: New languages born from contact — and the systematic structure of vernaculars

concepts.title: African American Vernacular English (AAVE)
concepts.contentHtml:
African American Vernacular English (AAVE) is a systematic, rule-governed variety of American English with a distinct grammar. Key features include:

  • Habitual 'be': 'She be working late' — a present tense not available in Standard American English; marks habitual or recurring action. 'She working late' (without 'be') means she is working late right now.
  • Copula deletion: 'He tall' (= He is tall). This deletion follows systematic rules and parallels features in Caribbean creoles.
  • Negative concord: 'I don't know nothing' — grammatically required double negative, not a logical error.

Labov's landmark 1972 work on AAVE demonstrated it is a coherent linguistic system, countering deficit theories that portrayed AAVE speakers as linguistically deficient.

concepts.title: Pidgins and Creoles
concepts.contentHtml:
A pidgin is a reduced contact language that develops when people who share no common language need to communicate. Pidgins have simplified grammar, limited vocabulary, and no native speakers. Tok Pisin (Papua New Guinea), West African Pidgin English.

When a pidgin becomes the first language of a community — when children grow up speaking it as their mother tongue — it creolizes into a full, complex language. A creole has the full grammatical complexity of any natural language: Haitian Creole, Jamaican Creole, Sranan Tongo.

Derek Bickerton's language bioprogram hypothesis proposed that creoles show similar grammatical features across unrelated substrate languages, suggesting children 'supply' innate grammar when input is impoverished. This is controversial but stimulating.

concepts.title: Standard Languages and Language Policy
concepts.contentHtml:
A standard language is a codified, prestige variety used in formal contexts — in education, government, media, and literature. Standard varieties are typically based on one regional dialect that gained prestige, usually the dialect of a political or cultural center.

Standardization involves: selection (which dialect?), codification (dictionaries, grammars), elaboration (expanding vocabulary for new domains), and acceptance (by the community).

Language policy governs official use of language. France's Académie Française actively polices vocabulary (resisting 'le email' in favor of courriel). India has 22 officially recognized languages. South Africa recognizes 11. Language policy reflects political negotiation about identity, inclusion, and power — never purely linguistic decisions.

title: Language Change, Spread, and the Future
description: How languages spread, how they change from within, and what the digital age means

concepts.title: Language Spread and Lingua Francas
concepts.contentHtml:
A lingua franca is a language used for communication between people who have different native languages. Throughout history, different languages have served this role:

  • Latin: medieval European scholarship and religion
  • Arabic: Islamic scholarship and trade, 8th–15th centuries
  • French: European diplomacy, 17th–19th centuries
  • English: global science, business, and internet communication today

English as a global lingua franca has produced World Englishes — distinct varieties like Indian English, Nigerian English, and Singaporean English (Singlish) that have their own grammatical and phonological norms. These are not 'broken' English — they are legitimate varieties with their own systematic rules.

concepts.title: How Language Change Spreads Through Communities
concepts.contentHtml:
Labov's research showed that language change is led by specific social groups and spreads through social networks. Key findings:

  • Changes are typically led by the second-highest status group (not the very top, who are conservative)
  • Women often lead changes in progress — especially changes from below (not consciously noticed)
  • Changes spread through social networks: tight-knit, dense networks (like working-class communities) resist change; loose-knit networks accelerate it

The S-curve of language change: a new feature spreads slowly at first, then rapidly, then slows as it reaches near-universal adoption — mirroring the spread of other social innovations. Sociolinguistics can measure ongoing changes in real time, tracking which forms will be standard English in 100 years.

concepts.title: Language in the Digital Age
concepts.contentHtml:
The internet and social media have created new linguistic registers, new forms of variation, and new sociolinguistic dynamics:

  • CMC (Computer-Mediated Communication) created new norms: abbreviations (lol, brb), emoji as paralinguistic cues, deliberately non-standard spelling for stylistic effect
  • Social media enables language communities to form and maintain varieties across geography — diaspora communities preserve heritage languages; fan communities develop shared registers
  • Platforms can accelerate or dampen language change: memes spread coinages globally in hours; algorithms may filter non-standard forms

Naomi Baron and David Crystal have written extensively on whether texting 'degrades' language. Linguistic consensus: no — each new medium develops appropriate registers. Texters are not losing literacy; they are code-switching into a new register.
